pieces.text: Read the following passage from

content.text: The Prince

pieces.text: by Niccolò Machiavelli. Machiavelli was a diplomat of the Florentine republic during the Italian Renaissance. He opens his treatise with this letter to Prince Lorenzo de' Medici, the newly crowned monarch of Florence. Throughout

content.text: The Prince

pieces.text: , Machiavelli speaks directly to Medici, offering him advice on governing.

textContent.text: People trying to attract the good will of a sovereign usually offer him something they care a lot about themselves, or something they've seen he particularly likes. So rulers are always being given horses, arms, gold brocades, jewels and whatever finery seems appropriate. Eager myself to bring Your Highness some token of my loyalty, I realized there was nothing more precious or important to me than my knowledge of great men and their doings, a knowledge gained through long experience of contemporary affairs and a constant study of ancient history. Having thought over all I've learned, and analyzed it with the utmost care, I've written everything down in a short book that I am now sending to Your Highness.

And though this gift is no doubt unworthy of you, I feel sure the experience it contains will make it welcome, especially when you think that I could hardly offer anything better than the chance to grasp in a few hours what I have discovered and assimilated over many years of danger and discomfort. I haven't prettified the book or padded it out with long sentences or pompous, pretentious words, or any of the irrelevant flourishes and attractions so many writers use; I didn't want it to please for anything but the range and seriousness of its subject matter. Nor, I hope, will you think it presumptuous that a man of low, really the lowest, station should set out to discuss the way princes ought to govern their peoples. Just as artists who draw landscapes get down in the valley to study the mountains and go up to the mountains to look down on the valley, so one has to be a prince to get to know the character of a people and a man of the people to know the character of a prince.

Your Highness, please take this small gift in the spirit in which it is given. Study it carefully and you will find that my most earnest wish is that you should achieve the greatness that your status and qualities promise. Then if, from the high peak of your position, you ever look down on those far below, you will see how very ungenerously and unfairly life continues to treat me.
<citation>From Niccolò Machiavelli and Tim Parks (translation), The Prince. Copyright 2009 by Tim Parks</citation>

pieces.text: Your Highness, please take this small gift in the spirit in which it is given. Study it carefully and you will find that my most earnest wish is that you should achieve the greatness that your status and qualities promise.

content.text: Then if, from the high peak of your position, you ever look down on those far below, you will see how very ungenerously and unfairly life continues to treat me.

contents.text: Machiavelli says that Medici should accept the book as a "gift," and that the ruler should study its contents in order to succeed. The text also declares that once Medici reaches the heights of his success, he will understand that Machiavelli has been mistreated. This narrative turn—describing the book both as a gift and as a way of revealing Machiavelli's misfortunes—suggests that Machiavelli's rhetorical purpose may be to provide Medici with guidance and counsel so that he can receive something in return.

contents.text: Machiavelli uses a simile to explain why his perspective should be valued by Medici. By comparing himself to a painter who stands in the valley to see the mountains above more clearly and fully, Machiavelli conveys that his common standing allows him to see the "whole picture" of Medici's character as a leader.

The figurative language implies that, because of their distance from, and perspective on, the ruling class, common people are able to judge rulers more objectively and accurately than other aristocrats.

contents.text: Machiavelli does this to establish his credibility:

text.text: He claims to have taken great risks over time to amass valuable knowledge about leadership.

content.text: Machiavelli values his knowledge of great leaders as much as others value horses, jewels, and finery. He says that he "could hardly offer anything better than the chance to grasp [what he has] discovered and assimilated over many years of danger and discomfort."

contents.text: Machiavelli does not do these things to establish credibility:

text.text: He claims to have traveled great distances to study the nature of successful rulers.

content.text: Machiavelli uses imagery of mountains and valleys to create a figurative comparison in the text; he does not use this language to make a literal claim about having traveled in order to attain knowledge.

text.text: He claims to use ornate language and a writing style that makes him superior to other writers.

content.text: While Machiavelli claims to be knowledgeable about "contemporary affairs," he does not name powerful men he has worked with, nor does he attempt to build credibility by establishing his relationship with powerful rulers.

So rulers are always being given horses, arms, gold brocades, jewels and whatever finery seems appropriate. Eager myself to bring Your Highness some token of my loyalty, I realized there was nothing more precious or important to me than my knowledge of great men and their doings, a knowledge gained through long experience of contemporary affairs and a constant study of ancient history. Having thought over all I've learned, and analyzed it with the utmost care, I've written everything down in a short book that I am now sending to Your Highness.

And though this gift is no doubt unworthy of you, I feel sure the experience it contains will make it welcome, especially when you think that I could hardly offer anything better than the chance to grasp in a few hours what I have discovered and assimilated over many years of danger and discomfort. I haven't prettified the book or padded it out with long sentences or pompous, pretentious words, or any of the irrelevant flourishes and attractions so many writers use; I didn't want it to please for anything but the range and seriousness of its subject matter. Nor, I hope, will you think it presumptuous that a man of low, really the lowest, station should set out to discuss the way princes ought to govern their peoples. Just as artists who draw landscapes get down in the valley to study the mountains and go up to the mountains to look down on the valley, so one has to be a prince to get to know the character of a people and a man of the people to know the character of a prince.

Your Highness, please take this small gift in the spirit in which it is given. Study it carefully and you will find that my most earnest wish is that you should achieve the greatness that your status and qualities promise. Then if, from the high peak of your position, you ever look down on those far below, you will see how very ungenerously and unfairly life continues to treat me.

contents.text: Machiavelli uses a metaphor about artists needing distance from their subjects to set up his claim about judgment. When he says that "one has to be a prince to get to know the character of the people," and vice versa, he is saying that the different social stations of princes and commoners allow them to truly see each other in ways they could not if they were closer in social position.
So, this detail suggests that Machiavelli believes that people are better at judging individuals from a different social class than they are at judging individuals from their own class.

So rulers are always being given horses, arms, gold brocades, jewels and whatever finery seems appropriate. Eager myself to bring Your Highness some token of my loyalty, I realized there was nothing more precious or important to me than my knowledge of great men and their doings, a knowledge gained through long experience of contemporary affairs and a constant study of ancient history. Having thought over all I've learned, and analyzed it with the utmost care, I've written everything down in a short book that I am now sending to Your Highness.

And though this gift is no doubt unworthy of you, I feel sure the experience it contains will make it welcome, especially when you think that I could hardly offer anything better than the chance to grasp in a few hours what I have discovered and assimilated over many years of danger and discomfort. I haven't prettified the book or padded it out with long sentences or pompous, pretentious words, or any of the irrelevant flourishes and attractions so many writers use; I didn't want it to please for anything but the range and seriousness of its subject matter. Nor, I hope, will you think it presumptuous that a man of low, really the lowest, station should set out to discuss the way princes ought to govern their peoples. Just as artists who draw landscapes get down in the valley to study the mountains and go up to the mountains to look down on the valley, so one has to be a prince to get to know the character of a people and a man of the people to know the character of a prince.

Your Highness, please take this small gift in the spirit in which it is given. Study it carefully and you will find that my most earnest wish is that you should achieve the greatness that your status and qualities promise. Then if, from the high peak of your position, you ever look down on those far below, you will see how very ungenerously and unfairly life continues to treat me.
<citation>From Niccolò Machiavelli and Tim Parks (translation), The Prince. Copyright 2009 by Tim Parks</citation>

contents.text: Machiavelli says that Medici should accept the book as a "gift," and that the ruler should study its contents in order to succeed. contents.text: Machiavelli uses a metaphor about artists needing distance from their subjects to set up his claim about judgment. When he says that "one has to be a prince to get to know the character of the people," and vice versa, he is saying that the different social stations of princes and commoners allow them to truly see each other in ways they could not if they were closer in social position.
So, this detail suggests that Machiavelli believes that people are better at judging individuals from a different social class than they are at judging individuals from their own class.

contents.text: Machiavelli uses a simile to explain why his perspective should be valued by Medici. By comparing himself to a painter who stands in the valley to see the mountains above more clearly and fully, Machiavelli conveys that his common standing allows him to see the "whole picture" of Medici's character as a leader.

The figurative language implies that, because of their distance from, and perspective on, the ruling class, common people are able to judge rulers more objectively and accurately than other aristocrats.

contents.text: Machiavelli does not do these things to establish credibility:

text.text: He claims to have traveled great distances to study the nature of successful rulers.

content.text: Machiavelli uses imagery of mountains and valleys to create a figurative comparison in the text; he does not use this language to make a literal claim about having traveled in order to attain knowledge.

text.text: He claims to use ornate language and a writing style that makes him superior to other writers.

content.text: Machiavelli says he has avoided using pretty language, long sentences, and "pompous, pretentious words" in order to keep the focus on the serious content of his book.

text.text: He claims to have taken on a wide range of responsibilities alongside many powerful rulers.

content.text: While Machiavelli claims to be knowledgeable about "contemporary affairs," he does not name powerful men he has worked with, nor does he attempt to build credibility by establishing his relationship with powerful rulers.

pieces.text: On one level,

content.text: The Prince

pieces.text: is a practical "how-to" manual for holding and expanding power. On another, it is an important work of political philosophy

contents.text: Machiavelli uses a metaphor about artists needing distance from their subjects to set up his claim about judgment. When he says that "one has to be a prince to get to know the character of the people," and vice versa, he is saying that the different social stations of princes and commoners allow them to truly see each other in ways they could not if they were closer in social position.
So, this detail suggests that Machiavelli believes that people are better at judging individuals from a different social class than they are at judging individuals from their own class.
